technique: Appears to be 3D CG animation (likely Blender/Cinema4D) using a felt/wool-fiber shader on the suit, sweater, and hair to fake a needle-felted stop-motion puppet look, rather than genuine practical stop-motion. Evidence: the overhead shot (periodic-4) glides in a perfectly smooth, floating dolly move with no set jitter or rig wobble, and the wide establishing shots keep flawlessly even studio lighting across every frame with zero flicker or dust/lint artifacts that would show up on a real tabletop set. The fiber texture itself (visible strand direction on the black suit and brown sweater) is a rendered fuzz/hair shader, not photographed felt. Characters are posed pose-to-pose with long static holds between key expressions, which is a deliberate stylistic choice layered on top of clean CG rather than an inherent stop-motion limitation. Flagging genuine uncertainty since a very well-executed miniature stop-motion rig could theoretically produce similar results.
facial_animation_notes: Mouth shapes are the primary moving facial element and cycle through only a handful of simple forms synced to dialogue: a flat closed line (periodic-8/9 neutral), a small pursed oval for 'NO.' (periodic-9/10), and a wider open rounded shape for exclamatory lines (periodic-3 'MINUTES'). Eyebrows do more emotional work than the mouth, snapping between a flat/raised 'blank' brow (periodic-1/2) and a sharply lowered, close-together scowl (periodic-6, periodic-9/10) with no visible in-between easing frame in the sampled set, suggesting a small library of brow shape-keys swapped rather than continuously deformed geometry.
eye_and_blink_notes: No blink was captured across any of the 15 periodic samples despite them spanning the full ~14s runtime; eyes stay open with a permanently heavy-lidded, half-closed upper lid that is a baked-in design trait (the 'low battery/tired' look) rather than an animated blink cycle. Gaze direction changes are handled by rotating the small fixed black pupil within the white sclera (compare periodic-9 vs periodic-10, where the pupils shift slightly without any lid movement). The one major eye event in the sampled frames is a graphic 'pop-open' take on the logo/outro close-up (scene-9), where both eyes go from droopy to fully round and bulging with visible sclera all around the pupil — a single dramatic pose swap, not a gradual widen.
head_movement_notes: Heads pivot as rigid units on a stiff neck with almost no secondary follow-through or overshoot; comparing periodic-8 and periodic-9 (both seated at the table) the head angle is essentially unchanged frame to frame, reinforcing a held-pose acting style. The clearest head movement is a downward/sideways tilt paired with the lowered scowl brow in the close-up (periodic-6), used to punctuate a line rather than as continuous motion.
gesture_notes: Gestures read as single graphic key poses held across multiple samples rather than continuously animated arcs: the crossed-arms defensive pose is essentially frozen from periodic-2 through periodic-3, the double open-palm 'shrug' during 'MINUTES' (periodic-3) is a flat, symmetric held pose, and the pointing arm toward the restaurant (periodic-6/periodic-7, seen from both front and back) does not visibly change position between the two samples. This pose-to-pose, low-frequency gesture style is consistent with deliberately sparse/limited animation for comedic deadpan timing.
idle_motion_notes: Between dialogue beats the characters show no visible idle sway, weight shift, or breathing motion — bodies look 'parked' in a pose (most evident in the seated periodic-8/periodic-9 pair, which are near-identical). The one passage of continuous idle-type motion is the walk to the table (scene-4), which shows a plausible alternating stride with arm counter-swing, suggesting a smoother rigged walk-cycle was used there in contrast to the otherwise static dialogue holds.
frame_rate_feel: Metadata reports 30fps, but the perceived animation feels much choppier than that: consecutive periodic keyframes sampled across the ~14.3s runtime frequently show almost no change in body pose (e.g., periodic-8 vs periodic-9, periodic-13 vs periodic-14), indicating the character performance is animated on long holds with only mouth/eyebrow updates in between, closer to a 2s-or-slower hold cadence layered on a 30fps render. Camera moves (the overhead push-in in periodic-4, dolly framing changes) read as smoothly interpolated by contrast, so the choppiness feels like a deliberate 'stuttering puppet' performance choice rather than a technical limitation of the render.
overall_animation_style_notes: The overall feel is graphic and deadpan: exaggeratedly long wedge-shaped noses and tiny bodies swallowed by an oversized black suit sit against a flat, evenly lit, pastel restaurant set with repeating tables/chairs, and symmetric or overhead compositions (periodic-1, periodic-4) give it an editorial, almost stop-motion-diorama look. Comedy is carried by held 'gag poses' and a sparse expression library (scowl brow, flat mouth, occasional wide-eyed take) rather than continuous nuanced motion, which matches a short-form social-video production pipeline (title-card intro/outro, on-screen caption text burned in per line, punchy character-swap holds) optimized for quick cuts rather than animated fluidity.
